hints: Focus on what a C=C double bond in an alkene is really made of, not just calling it a double bond.
Remember that the $\pi$ bond is weaker and more exposed, so it is the part that opens up while the $\sigma$ framework stays intact.
Now think about how the monomers join together, what kind of single new link forms between one carbon and the next?
walkthrough:
**Recall the structure of the alkene double bond**

Think of C=C as two bonds in one. There is a strong $\sigma$ bond directly between the carbons, plus a weaker $\pi$ bond above and below.

$$\text{C=C consists of: 1 } \sigma \text{ bond + 1 } \pi \text{ bond}$$

**Work out what is broken**

In addition polymerisation the double bond opens out to become single. The strong $\sigma$ bond stays, only the weaker $\pi$ bond breaks to free two electrons for new bonding.

$$\text{C=C (} \sigma + \pi \text{) } \rightarrow \text{ -C-C- unit with } \sigma \text{ left, } \pi \text{ broken}$$

**Work out what is formed**

Those freed electrons form new single bonds linking one monomer to the next. A single C-C link between monomers is a $\sigma$ bond only, no new $\pi$ bond is made.

$$\text{n CH}_2\text{=CH}_2 \rightarrow \text{-[CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{]-}_n \text{ by new C-C } \sigma \text{ bonds}$$

**Put it together**

Broken: $\pi$ only. Formed: $\sigma$ only. That matches the $\pi$ only broken, $\sigma$ only formed row.

options.A: Correct. Each alkene C=C has $\sigma + \pi$. Only the $\pi$ part breaks, leaving the $\sigma$ intact, and monomers join by new C-C $\sigma$ single bonds. So $\pi$ only broken, $\sigma$ only formed.
options.B: Incorrect. It is right that only $\pi$ is broken, but no new $\pi$ bond is formed. The polymer backbone is all single C-C bonds, which are $\sigma$ only. Students choose this by thinking a double bond must reform.
options.C: Incorrect. The $\sigma$ bond in C=C is not broken, it remains as the C-C $\sigma$ bond in the polymer chain. Students choose this by thinking the whole double bond breaks apart completely.
options.D: Incorrect. Neither part is correct as stated. Only $\pi$ breaks (not $\sigma$), and only $\sigma$ forms (not $\pi$). Students choose this by confusing breaking the C=C with breaking both components and reforming both.
